query: According to Paul Graham, what should founders do to recruit their very first users?
expected_answer: Founders have to manually recruit users themselves rather than waiting for users to come to them. PG cites Stripe's aggressive early user acquisition -- the 'Collison installation' technique, where instead of just offering a beta signup link, the founders personally sat down with a candidate user and got the product installed and working on the spot.

title: How biotech startup funding will change in the next 10 years
source: https://www.ycombinator.com/library/4L-how-biotech-startup-funding-will-change-in-the-next-10-years
---  
Back when YC was getting started about 10 years ago, Paul Graham wrote [some](http://www.paulgraham.com/webstartups.html) [essays](http://www.paulgraham.com/future.html) that predicted the way startup fundraising would change in the next decade - accurately, it turns out. Paul Graham predicted that there would be way more startups, that they’d be cheaper to start, that new kinds of investors would fund them, that founders would be more technical, and that founders would keep control of their companies. All of those seem to have come true.  
I've noticed that raising money for a biotech or other life science[1](#footnote1) company in 2019 looks a lot like raising money for a tech company 10 years ago. Since then, fundamental forces caused fundraising for tech companies to change dramatically. I see those same forces that Paul Graham wrote about happening with biotech companies now. And I believe that they are going to change biotech fundraising very much the way they changed tech company fundraising.

From source corpus\yc_library\do-things-that-don-t-scale.md: There are two reasons founders resist going out and recruiting users individually. One is a combination of shyness and laziness. They'd rather sit at home writing code than go out and talk to a bunch of strangers and probably be rejected by most of them. But for a startup to succeed, at least one founder (usually the CEO) will have to spend a lot of time on sales and marketing. [2]  
The other reason founders ignore this path is that the absolute numbers seem so small at first. This can't be how the big, famous startups got started, they think. The mistake they make is to underestimate the power of compound growth. We encourage every startup to measure their progress by weekly [growth rate](http://www.paulgraham.com/growth.html). If you have 100 users, you need to get 10 more next week to grow 10% a week. And while 110 may not seem much better than 100, if you keep growing at 10% a week you'll be surprised how big the numbers get. After a year you'll have 14,000 users, and after 2 years you'll have 2 million.

From source corpus\yc_library\do-things-that-don-t-scale.md: How do you find users to recruit manually? If you build something to solve [your own problems](http://www.paulgraham.com/startupideas.html), then you only have to find your peers, which is usually straightforward. Otherwise you'll have to make a more deliberate effort to locate the most promising vein of users. The usual way to do that is to get some initial set of users by doing a comparatively untargeted launch, and then to observe which kind seem most enthusiastic, and seek out more like them. For example, Ben Silbermann noticed that a lot of the earliest Pinterest users were interested in design, so he went to a conference of design bloggers to recruit users, and that worked well. [5]

From source corpus\yc_library\do-things-that-don-t-scale.md: Another consulting-like technique for recruiting initially lukewarm users is to use your software yourselves on their behalf. We did that at Viaweb. When we approached merchants asking if they wanted to use our software to make online stores, some said no, but they'd let us make one for them. Since we would do anything to get users, we did. We felt pretty lame at the time. Instead of organizing big strategic e-commerce partnerships, we were trying to sell luggage and pens and men's shirts. But in retrospect it was exactly the right thing to do, because it taught us how it would feel to merchants to use our software. Sometimes the feedback loop was near instantaneous: in the middle of building some merchant's site I'd find I needed a feature we didn't have, so I'd spend a couple hours implementing it and then resume building the site.

response:
Based on Paul Graham's essay "Do Things That Don't Scale," here are his key recommendations for founders recruiting their very first users:

## Main Approach: Manual, Individual Recruitment

Graham emphasizes that founders should **go out and recruit users individually**, even though this doesn't scale. He acknowledges two reasons founders resist this:
1. **Shyness and laziness** - it's easier to stay home coding than talk to strangers who may reject you
2. **Underestimating compound growth** - the small initial numbers seem insignificant

However, he stresses that **at least one founder (usually the CEO) needs to spend significant time on sales and marketing** for the startup to succeed.

## Strategies for Finding Users:

1. **Build for your own problems first** - If you solve your own problems, you only need to find your peers, which is straightforward.

2. **Launch to identify your most enthusiastic user segment** - Do an initial broad launch, then observe which types of users are most enthusiastic and seek out more like them. Graham's example: Pinterest founder Ben Silbermann noticed early users were interested in design, so he recruited at design blogger conferences.

3. **Do the work yourself if needed** - At Viaweb, when potential customers were reluctant, Graham's team would actually build the online stores for them. This taught them how customers would experience the software and provided instant feedback for feature development.

The key insight is that **compound growth from consistent weekly user acquisition** will eventually lead to massive numbers - growing 10% weekly yields 14,000 users after a year and 2 million after two years.
